explain.say: Each time the skin moves out it squashes the air next to it, and each time it moves back it stretches the air. These squeezes and stretches are passed from air molecule to air molecule.

faq.a: Every sound is made by something vibrating, moving quickly back and forth: a drum skin, a guitar string, your vocal folds or a bee's wings. The vibration pushes on the air around it.
asks: Why does a drum make a noise?

faq.q: Does air move from the drum to me?
faq.a: No. Each air molecule only jiggles a tiny distance back and forth. What travels to you is the pattern of squeezes and stretches, the way a ripple moves across a pond while the water stays put.
asks: Does sound move air across a room?
Do air particles travel with sound?

faq.a: A sound wave is a travelling pattern of high pressure, called compressions, and low pressure, called rarefactions. Because the air moves back and forth in the same direction the wave travels, it is a longitudinal wave.
asks: What kind of wave is sound?

faq.q: How fast does sound travel in air?
faq.a: About 343 metres per second in air at 20 degrees Celsius, roughly a kilometre every three seconds. It goes a little faster in warm air and slower in cold air.
asks: What is the speed of sound?
How long does sound take to travel a kilometre?

faq.q: How does my ear turn a wave into sound?
faq.a: The wave pushes your eardrum in and out. Three tiny bones pass the movement to the fluid-filled cochlea, where hair cells turn it into nerve signals for your brain.

facts: Sound travels at about 343 metres per second in air at 20 degrees Celsius.
Sound in air is a longitudinal wave: the air moves back and forth along the direction the wave travels.
